seoTitle: Best Free App to Bulk Edit Prices on Shopify
metaDescription: Use a free bulk price editor app on Shopify to increase or decrease product prices by percentage across your entire catalog fast.
intro: Changing prices on a Shopify store one product page at a time falls apart the moment you have more than a handful of SKUs — a storewide sale or a supplier cost increase can mean touching hundreds of variants by hand. A bulk price editor app fixes that by letting you target a field, set a percentage or fixed change, and apply it across your whole catalog or a single collection in one pass. This guide walks through Bulk Price Editor Sami, a free app built for exactly this job, from installing it to running your first bulk task and catching the most common reason edits appear to fail.

steps.heading: Install the app from the Shopify App Store
steps.body: Search the Shopify App Store for "Bulk Price Editor Sami" and click install. Shopify will show a permissions screen listing exactly what the app can see and change — in this case, your store owner's personal data and the ability to view and edit product data, since that's what a price editor needs to do its job. Read the requested scopes before approving; a price tool only needs product access, not customer or order data, so that's a reasonable ask here. Once you approve, the app installs and adds its own section to your Shopify admin sidebar, below your regular Apps list.

image.caption: The install prompt for Bulk Price Editor Sami, showing the personal-data and store-data permissions it requests before setup.

steps.heading: Create a bulk edit task
steps.body: Open the app and start a new task. Give it a name you'll recognize later — something like "Bulk increase by 10%" rather than the default placeholder, since you may end up running several of these over time and want to tell them apart in a history list. Under Field to edit, choose Price (the app can also target other product fields). Then pick an edit method: increase or decrease by a percentage, or set a fixed value, and enter the number. A rounding option lets you round results to the nearest cent or nearest whole number, which matters if a percentage change produces an odd number like $23.0999.

image.caption: The Create task screen: a 10% price increase set up with rounding to the nearest .01 and the compare-at price left untouched.

steps.heading: Decide what happens to compare-at price
steps.body: Right below the rounding setting, the task form asks whether to leave the compare-at price alone or set it explicitly. This is worth stopping on: if you're running a genuine discount, you likely want the compare-at price to show the old, higher amount so customers see the strikethrough savings at checkout. If you're just correcting your regular price after a cost change, leaving compare-at untouched is usually right. Getting this wrong is a common source of a sale that either shows no discount at all or shows a discount you didn't intend.

steps.heading: Preview the calculated prices before saving
steps.body: Rather than running the task blind, the app lets you review a results table with columns for the product, its original price, and the updated price it's about to apply — so you can catch a bad multiplier or a rounding surprise before it goes live on the storefront. In the example run shown here, a set of $21.00 variants were about to move to $23.10 apiece, and a $20.99 variant to $23.09, all visible in the same table before confirming. Scroll through a representative sample of the list, not just the first row, since a percentage change can behave unexpectedly on very low- or very high-priced items.

image.caption: The task results table listing each variant's original price next to its updated price, ready to check before the change goes live.

steps.heading: Schedule the change and set an auto-revert
steps.body: For time-limited promotions, use the Start time and Revert time controls on the task form instead of running the edit manually twice. Set Start time to a future date to have the price change apply automatically when a sale begins, and check Schedule the revert to have prices snap back to their original values the moment the promotion ends — no need to remember to undo anything at midnight. This scheduling and auto-revert pair is the difference between a bulk editor you use occasionally and one you can build a recurring sales calendar around.

steps.heading: Troubleshoot a bulk edit that isn't updating
steps.body: If prices don't change after you run a task, check the field mapping first — it's easy to select the wrong field or apply the edit method to compare-at price when you meant regular price. Next, confirm the task actually finished; large catalogs can take a few minutes to process, and the app's task list will show a status rather than an instant result. If specific products were excluded, check whether they're tagged, filtered out, or in a collection that wasn't included in the task's scope. Re-running the task on a small test collection first is the fastest way to isolate which of these is the culprit before touching your whole catalog again.

faq.question: Can I undo a bulk price change if I make a mistake?
faq.answer: Yes, if you scheduled a revert time when creating the task, prices roll back automatically. If you didn't, most bulk editor apps including this one keep a record of the original prices in the task history, so you can create a follow-up task to restore them.

faq.question: Will bulk editing affect sale or compare-at prices too?
faq.answer: That depends on the choice you make on the task form — you can explicitly set the compare-at price during the edit, or choose "Don't change compare-at price" to leave it as-is while only the regular price changes.

faq.question: Is a free bulk price editor limited in how many products it can update?
faq.answer: Free plans on apps like this typically cap the number of products or tasks per month, so check the app's current limits in its pricing tab if you're planning to update a very large catalog.

faq.question: Can I apply price changes to just one collection instead of the whole store?
faq.answer: Yes — when creating a task you can scope it to a specific collection or a filtered set of products rather than applying the edit to everything in your store.

faq.question: Why didn't my bulk price edit apply to some products?
faq.answer: The most common causes are selecting the wrong field to edit, a task that's still processing on a large catalog, or products that were filtered out of the task's scope. Running the edit on a small test collection first makes it easy to confirm the setup is correct.
